newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo court fines DKB for breaking banking law.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo court fines DKB for breaking banking law.

text.p: One of Japan's top commercial banks, Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB), was fined 500,000 yen ($4,273) by Tokyo Summary Court on Monday for hiding loans to a racketeer -- the first time such a penalty has been imposed.
Court officials said the court accepted prosecutors' recommendation on the size of the fine, the maximum allowed for such a violation.

The move comes ahead of an expected announcement this week of administrative penalties against DKB and giant brokerage Nomura Securities Co Ltd, both entangled in a high-profile scandal involving payoffs to a "sokaiya" corporate racketeer.

Vice Finance Minister Takeshi Komura told a news conference on Monday afternoon that the ministry's penalties would be decided within a matter of days, adding that the ministry planned to take stern steps against both companies.
DKB's violations of the Banking Law "severely hindered the ministry's supervision and also damaged DKB's standing among the public and was very regrettable", Komura said.

In a statement, DKB said it took the most recent action against it "gravely," and added that it apologised deeply to all those whose trust it had breached in the incident, including shareholders, depositors and monetary authorities.

More than a dozen people including top executives from the two financial firms have been arrested in the affair, which coincides with the start of "Big Bang" reforms aimed at introducing more competition and global standards into Japan's long-sheltered financial sector.

The Finance Ministry on Friday filed a complaint with prosecutors against DKB and four former officials of the bank alleging they had hidden information about problem loans to sokaiya Ryuichi Koike during a ministry inspection in October 1994.
But Kunihiro Matsuo, the deputy chief Tokyo district prosecutor, said on Monday they were not indicting the four former DKB officials for Banking Law violations.

"The four individuals have already been indicted on the more serious charges of violating the Commercial Code, so we decided to forgo the indictment on the Banking Law," Matsuo told a news conference.
On Friday prosecutors indicted former DKB chairman Tadashi Okuda for extending 11.78 billion yen ($100 million) in loans to Koike through an affiliated firm.

Payoffs to sokaiya, racketeers who buy shares in companies and try to extort money by threatening to expose dubious business practices or who are sometimes employed by firms to quash questions from legitimate shareholders at annual meetings, have been illegal since 1983.
But many Japanese companies have found it difficult to cut off ties with the underworld.
Critics say lightweight penalties for violating banking, securities and commercial laws have failed to serve as deterrents for misdeeds, and politicians are urging stiffer punishments.

Concern, meanwhile, persists that the scandal could spread to other financial firms. Spokesmen for the rest of Japan's "Big Four" brokerages -- Daiwa Securities, Nikko Securities and Yamaichi Securities -- on Friday declined comment on a report that Tokyo prosecutors were poised to join the government securities watchdog in probing the three companies for evidence of illegal deals with Koike. ($1=117 yen)
